---
title: "Workflow graphs"
description: "Draws diagrams of a repository's GitHub Actions workflows into .github/workflow-graphs/README.md."
---

`workflow-graphs.yml` draws diagrams of your repository's GitHub Actions
workflows and keeps them up to date in `.github/workflow-graphs/README.md`.
GitHub shows that file when someone opens the `.github/workflow-graphs/`
folder, next to `.github/workflows/` — close to where people look to
understand how the repository's automation works, without cluttering the
README for your package's users.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why not inside `.github/workflows/`?
GitHub treats every file in `.github/workflows/` as a workflow file, and a
GitHub App may only change those with an extra *Workflows* permission —
which would also let it change your actual workflows. A folder of its own
needs no such permission.
:::

The diagrams are generated from the workflow files alone, with no AI
involved: the same files always give the same diagrams.

## What you get

- **A table** of all workflows — name, file, what starts them, which
  reusable workflows they call (with owner, repository, file and
  version), and what they produce, with the condition where there is one
  ("Issue for the PR author — *if check fails*"). The quickest way in.
- **One small diagram per situation** — a pull request into `dev`, a pull
  request into `main`, a closed pull request, a schedule, a push: the
  workflows it starts, the workflows those start in turn (dotted arrows),
  and what comes out of it, with conditions on the arrows. A workflow
  with several triggers appears in each.
- **One diagram per workflow**, in the order they come into play: its
  jobs in the order they run, with the result each waits for (success,
  failure). A job that calls a reusable workflow is opened up to show
  that workflow's jobs and their steps, so you see what actually happens.
  Conditions are written in words where possible, e.g. "only on
  schedule" or "skipped for PRs from bot-suggest/ branches".

GitHub draws the diagrams itself ([Mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org)), so
the README is plain text: changes show up as readable diffs.

## What workflows produce

What a workflow produces can't be read from its YAML reliably, so it is
described in `config/workflow-outcomes.yml` of this repository — for all
workflows here. Workflows that aren't listed simply get no outcome boxes.
To describe your own workflows, put a copy of that file at the same path
in your repository ([as for the other settings](suggestions.qmd#adjusting-the-guidance))
and add them, e.g. `.github/workflows/deploy.yml: [commit]` or your own
wording, `.github/workflows/deploy.yml: ["Site deployed to {environment}"]`
— `{environment}` is filled in from the calling job's input of that name.
Conditions under which a job runs are added automatically.

## Your own text is kept

The diagrams sit between marker comments such as
`<!-- workflow-graphs:overview:start -->`. Only those blocks are ever
replaced. The first run writes a short introduction around them; after
that, everything outside the blocks is yours:

- **Text below a workflow's diagram belongs to that workflow** and moves
  with it, as the workflows are always shown in the order they come into
  play. Write explanations of a workflow right below its diagram.
- **Text above the first workflow, and any section after them** that
  starts with a `#` or `##` heading, stays where it is — e.g. the
  introduction, or a closing "## Notes" section.
- A new workflow is added in its place in the order. When a workflow is
  deleted, its diagram goes, but the text you wrote below it is kept,
  after the last workflow.

## When it runs

| Event | What happens |
|---|---|
| Push to the branch where merges land (e.g. `dev`) | The README is updated and committed directly: `docs: update workflow diagrams`. A `docs:` commit never triggers a release. |
| Pull request | Nothing is committed. A comment shows how the PR changes the diagrams, updated on further pushes. |
| Manual run | Like a push, on the branch you pick. |

The example below runs on changes to `.github/workflows/` only. The README
lives outside that folder, so updating it doesn't start another run.

::: {.callout-note}
## Protected branch
If the branch requires pull requests, the direct commit needs to bypass
that rule: add the [GitHub App](getting-started.qmd#github-app) as a bypass
actor for that branch, as for `main` in the
[release](branch-protection.qmd).
:::

## Chains between workflows

To find where one workflow starts another, the called reusable workflows
are read too, at the version you reference. Found are `workflow_run`
triggers, and dispatches sent with `gh api …/dispatches`,
`gh workflow run` or the common dispatch actions. A dispatch sent in
another way — or from inside a composite action — shows no arrow. A
called workflow in a private repository the job can't read is still shown,
marked "not readable".
